history.heading: Ancient and Ottoman era
paragraphs: Eritrea's Red Sea coast and highlands were part of the trade networks of the ancient world. The port of Adulis served the Kingdom of Aksum, which adopted Christianity in the 4th century. The highlands were later linked to Abyssinian kingdoms, while the Ottomans controlled the coast, including Massawa, from the 16th century.

history.heading: Italian colony
paragraphs: Italy established the colony of Eritrea in 1890, naming it after the Latin for Red Sea (Mare Erythraeum). Italian settlers built roads, a railway and the capital Asmara, whose modernist architecture of the 1930s is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Eritrean soldiers (askari) served in Italy's colonial wars.
Britain took control in 1941 during the Second World War.

history.heading: Struggle for independence
paragraphs: In 1952 the UN federated Eritrea with Ethiopia, which annexed it outright in 1962. An armed struggle for independence followed, lasting 30 years, eventually led by the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF). The EPLF took Asmara in 1991, and after a referendum Eritrea became independent on 24 May 1993, with Isaias Afwerki as president.
A border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 killed tens of thousands; peace was only signed in 2018. Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces in the Tigray war of 2020–2022.

culture.heading: Peoples and faiths
paragraphs: Eritrea has nine recognised ethnic groups, the largest being the Tigrinya and Tigre. Tigrinya, Arabic and English are the main working languages. The population is roughly divided between Christians, mainly Eritrean Orthodox, and Sunni Muslims.

Injera, a spongy flatbread, served with spicy stews such as zigni, is the staple food, and coffee ceremonies are an important social ritual. Italian influence lives on in cafés, pasta and cycling, which is a national passion.

politics.heading: One-party state
paragraphs: Eritrea is a one-party state ruled by President Isaias Afwerki and the People's Front for Democracy and Justice since independence. No national elections have been held, the 1997 constitution was never implemented, and there is no independent press.

Indefinite compulsory national service, which can last many years, has driven hundreds of thousands of Eritreans to flee abroad. Human rights organisations report severe repression. Tensions with Ethiopia have risen again over Ethiopia's desire for access to the sea.

economy.heading: A closed economy
paragraphs: Eritrea's economy is largely state-controlled and isolated. Most people depend on subsistence farming and herding. Mining of gold, copper and zinc, especially at the Bisha mine, provides most exports. Remittances from the diaspora are important.
The currency is the nakfa. Limited data are available, but Eritrea is among the world's poorest countries.
